"The meaning of the lotus emerging from the water is that one has irreversibly emerged from the muddy waters of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Entering into the great assembly of the Tathāgata, one sits as the various bodhisattvas sit upon lotuses, hearing the teaching of supreme, pure wisdom. This certainly does not mean sitting upon the petals of the flower.

It is simply that all these bodhisattvas, having heard the teaching of the one perfect path and realized the one perfect fruit, dwell in the realm of the Flower King and sit together with Śākyamuni Buddha upon the lotus pedestal.
Such was the Buddha’s intention.
Those who first beheld my body and initially heard the One Reality had already entered the lotus pedestal.
For those who have not yet entered, I proceed from the sudden to the gradual, employing further diverse skillful means to assist in the manifestation of the primary truth.

The various teachings on the two truths—whether presented singly, in combination, or as inconceivable—are all diverse in their forms, yet they are all skillful means for the sake of the lotus pedestal.

Yet the Tathāgata is eternally quiescent, yet his transformation pervades the entire Dharma-realm; in reality, he makes no discrimination, nor does he act after prior deliberation. By the power of the roots of goodness of this compassionate guidance, he enables all sentient beings to enter therein from this point.
Some say: "From the Deer Park onwards, all [teachings] were merely introductory preludes to the Lotus Sūtra.
Now it is said that this is not so.

Furthermore, from the recent discourse on the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) onwards, all has served as a preliminary lead-in to the Lotus Sūtra; thus, the illumination of other lands and the manifestation of Buddhas therein are entirely intended to suddenly open up the gradual teachings.
Mañjuśrī leads the way for the Buddhas of the past and likewise opens up the sudden and the gradual.

Although such introductory maneuvers are still considered too proximate, from the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū onwards, he has employed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as a skillful means for sentient beings; one should know that this does not stop at being merely proximate to the site of enlightenment.
Furthermore, this is still relatively recent; since attaining Buddhahood in the beginning, he has employed the skillful means of the lotus pedestal for the sake of sentient beings.
Moreover, it is even more recent; since originally practicing the bodhisattva path, he has employed the skillful means of the lotus pedestal for the sake of sentient beings.
The text says:
"I originally established a vow that all sentient beings everywhere shall likewise attain this Way.
One should know that this preliminary introduction did not begin only with the present!

Those originally transformed to enter the flower pedestal constitute one side; as for those who have not yet entered, they do not cease their application of the aforementioned skillful means, and it is likewise in the interim.

If one enters the Flower Terrace from sutras such as the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Vaipulya*, or the *Prajñāpāramitā*—whether by entering the Shared or Perfect [vehicles] from the Shared, or entering the Shared or Perfect from the Distinct—this is no different from those who enter it directly; furthermore, each constitutes its own particular side.
Those who have not yet entered, having been matured by the four flavors, shall all enter the lotus pedestal through this sutra.

Among the various teachings, whether they abide in three flavors, two flavors, or one flavor, or remain entirely unripened, all shall have their coarseness resolved into the sublime and enter the lotus pedestal.

The Tripitaka masters preserve the fruits [of their realization]; that which was difficult to break they have already broken, and that which was difficult to open they have already opened—how much more so for that which is easy to break and easy to open? All follow their dispositions while remaining rooted in the fundamental; by manifesting the reality at the very gate, they immediately enter the lotus pedestal.
The text states:
"There are immeasurable numbers of great carriages made of the seven treasures, each to be bestowed upon the sons.
This passage, and others like it, represents the opening of the provisional to reveal the real; all that is coarse is shown to be wondrous, which is the wondrousness of absolute transcendence.

As stated above, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* subsumes all scriptures; herein the matter reaches its ultimate limit, representing the fundamental intent of the Buddha’s appearance in the world and the final destination of all teachings.

If people do not perceive this principle, they regard these as mere phenomena arising from causes and conditions; their contemptuousness does not cease, and their tongues will rot within their mouths.

If one grasps the essential intent, one will deeply perceive the seven kinds and twenty-one varieties of immeasurable teaching-gates. Their significance is vast and far-reaching, mutually interpenetrating; they are as intricate and subtle as embroidery, extending horizontally and penetrating vertically, all ultimately converging in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The teachings established by twenty thousand luminous Buddhas, such as Kāśyapa and others of antiquity, reached their ultimate excellence here.
A sutra states:
"When Maitreya comes in the future, his teachings shall likewise reach their ultimate excellence here."
Śākyamuni’s upward conformity with the three periods of time is likewise most wondrously consummate herein.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*’s "ransoming life" and "precious treasure" are merely heavy slaps on the palm.
Contemplating this wondrous purport, its grandeur is all-encompassing; those who seek it must broaden their minds and not confine that Great Void with human sentiments.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* elucidates the meaning of the ten superior characteristics (*daśa-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), which all have been regarded as reaching the ultimate depth, thereby causing the *Dilun* school to overturn its fundamental tenets.
Now, let us tentatively compare these with the Ten Subtleties (*daśa-miao*); therein, the former leaves something unaccounted for.

Furthermore, employing the subtlety of principle to compare it with the superior characteristics of the basis (āśraya), one clarifies the four propositions of inconceivable dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) to shatter attachments; how could one then retain the ālayavijñāna or the amala-vijñāna as the basis?

The establishment of the four *siddhāntas* does not merely posit the single phrase "ignorance arises from another"; rather, that directly constitutes the meaning of the single path of illumination. It does not fail to perceive the opening and closing of various sutras—whether sudden or gradual—for the sake of sentient beings; whether categorized by teaching or by practice; whether according to sentiment or according to wisdom—it broadly encompasses the Buddha’s transformation and deeply subsumes the beginning and the end.
Regarding the single object of conditions (*pratyaya*), I have already explained it extensively in relation to the basis (*āśraya*).

If one further attempts to apply analogies such as the fourfold Four Truths, the sevenfold Two Truths, the fivefold Three Truths, or the Single Truth, there would be no standard of comparison for them.
The ten wonders within the traces have already been partially revealed; however, the ten wonders within the fundamental source are not found even in the various sutras, let alone in those treatises.
Furthermore, the ten wonders of contemplating the mind can be immediately put into practice, unlike a poor man who merely counts the beads of a rosary of jewels.
One should know that these ten wondrous Dharma-gates are layered and accumulated one upon another; how could they ever be fully described!
Even the *Mahā-śāstra* of India does not belong to their class, so what need is there to mention the teachers of this land of China?
This is not intended as a boastful display of doctrinal characteristics; it is simply the natural state of things.
Reflect upon this for yourself; there is no need for prolixity.

Regarding the five vidyās and the three truths, their meanings are fully contained within the various sūtras, yet the specific names originate from the *Śrīkūṭa* (Sengluo) and the *Rājanirdeśa* (Renwang), which speak of the truth of existence, the truth of non-existence, and the supreme truth of the middle way.
This scripture also contains this meaning; the "Life Span" chapter states:
"Neither identical nor different" is the Middle Way.
"Identical" refers to the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), while "different" refers to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Question:
If this sutra does not contain the names of the four kinds of causes and conditions and so forth, why employ their meanings?
Answer:
The "five abodes" and "two deaths" are named after the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*; their meaning should not be applied to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
If one does not employ the five abodes, then ignorance (avidyā) cannot be destroyed.
If one does not employ the two types of death, then it would not be permanent.
Furthermore, the names of the three Buddhas appear in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*; otherwise, other sūtras would lack the meaning of the three Buddhas.
All the various sutras are spoken by the Buddha; though their names differ, their meaning must not be obstructed, and so forth.
Now, I shall clarify the three truths as threefold:
first, the clarification of the three truths.
2. Judging the coarse and the subtle.
3. Opening up the coarse to reveal the subtle.

Setting aside the previous two types of the Two Truths because they do not clarify the Middle Way, one can discuss the Middle Way by means of the five types of the Two Truths; thus, there are five types of the Three Truths.
By taking the specific and entering into the general, and by identifying that which is neither with-outflows nor without-outflows, the meaning of the three truths is established:
that which has outflows is the "conventional" (saṃvṛti);
that which is without outflows is the "ultimate" (paramārtha).
That which is neither with outflows nor without outflows is the "Middle.
In the *Śāstra on Teaching*, it differs from emptiness only in that the Middle lacks effort and does not encompass all phenomena.
Regarding "perfectly entering and penetrating the three truths": the two truths are no different from those previously mentioned;
however, the point that it is neither outflowing nor non-outflowing, yet possesses all dharmas, differs from the previous [explanation of] the middle truth.

Regarding the distinct three truths (*tri-satya*) of the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*): the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is divided into two truths, which, in contrast to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), constitute the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*).
This "middle" refers merely to principle (*li*), and so forth.

Regarding the Perfect Teaching’s (*pariniṣpanna*) entry into the three truths of the Separate Teaching: the two truths are no different from those previously mentioned; however, by adding the true and middle aspects, they are made to be fully endowed with the Buddha-dharma.

Regarding the perfect integration of the three truths (*triratna-satya*): it is not only the Middle Way that is fully endowed with the Buddha-dharma; the Truth of Reality (*satya*) and the Truth of Phenomena (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are likewise so.
The three truths are perfectly interfused such that one is three and three is one, as explained at length in the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation).

Second, regarding the judgment of the coarse and the subtle: the Separate [Vehicle] and the Perfect [Vehicle] that enter the Shared [Vehicle], as they still carry the expedient means of the Shared, are considered coarse;

the Separate [Vehicle] that does not carry the Shared is considered subtle. When the Perfect [Vehicle] enters the Separate [Vehicle] and carries the expedient means of the Separate, it is considered coarse; [the Perfect Vehicle that does not so carry them is subtle].
The Perfect Teaching (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*), which does not involve expedient means, is the most subtle and wondrous.
According to the five-flavored teachings, the Milk Teaching explains three kinds of the Three Truths: two are coarse and one is subtle.
The Curd Teaching consists only of the coarse and lacks the subtle.
Raw ghee and refined ghee both possess five kinds of the three truths—four coarse and one subtle.
This sutra possesses only one kind of the three truths, which is the subtle truth of mutual relativity (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Third, "opening the coarse to reveal the subtle": this means resolving all the aforementioned coarse levels into a single subtle truth. Since the three truths have nothing further upon which to depend, this is called the "subtle truth of the absolute.
Sixth, explaining the "single truth," the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"That which is called the two truths are in reality one; they are spoken of as two only as a skillful means."
It is like one who is intoxicated and has not yet vomited [the poison], who sees the sun and moon revolving and thus claims there are both a revolving sun and a non-revolving sun.
A sober person sees only that which does not revolve and does not see the revolution.
To transform the two [vehicles] is considered coarse, while not transforming them is considered sublime.
The Tripiṭaka consists entirely of the transformation of the two, making it similar to that intoxicated man.
The various Mahāyāna sūtras involve the transformation of the two while teaching the non-transformation of the one.
Now, this sutra directly abandons expedient means and speaks only of the unsurpassed path; because it does not deviate from the single reality, it is "wondrous.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* elucidates the characteristics and meanings of the stages, explaining the dharma of resemblance.
The "ground" (bhūmi) has the meaning of clarity regarding reality, as it explains the true Dharma.

Furthermore, the skillful means of the teaching gate has the meaning of clarity regarding the path of teaching, while that which explains the Dharma realized through practice has the meaning of clarity regarding the path of realization.
I shall now borrow this [passage]:
"After a long time, the Buddhas must speak the truth," which refers to the meaning of the reality of the ground (*bhūmi*).
"The Dharma attained at the site of enlightenment" refers to the meaning of the clarity of realized path; therefore, it is wondrous.
To cling to this as real is to make true speech into false speech; because such clinging gives rise to views regarding speech, it is called "coarse.
To be harmoniously integrated and free from attachment is therefore called "sublime."
It can be understood that the coarse is opened up to reveal the subtle, and so forth.

As for the fact that the various truths are ineffable: since "all dharmas from the very beginning have always been characterized by quiescence," how could there be the various truths with their manifold characteristics obstructing one another?
If even a single truth does not exist, how could there be any truths?
Each and every one is ineffable; that which can be expressed is coarse, while that which cannot be expressed is subtle.
Even the ineffability of the ineffable is subtle, for that which is subtle is itself subtle, as the path of language is severed.
If one speaks generally of that which is ineffable, then arising-and-arising is ineffable, up to and including non-arising-and-non-arising being ineffable.
The former ineffability is considered coarse, while the ineffability of non-arising-and-non-arising is considered sublime.
If the coarse and the subtle are distinct, they are mutually dependent and lack integration;
when the coarse and the subtle are non-dual, this is the "subtle that transcends dependence," and so forth.
Regarding the teachings of the five flavors: in the Milk Teaching, there is one aspect of the coarse without truth and one aspect of the subtle without truth.

In the teaching on curdled milk (*dadhi*), there is one coarse aspect that is without truth and one subtle aspect that is without truth. In the teaching on fresh butter (*navanīta*), there are three coarse aspects that are without truth and one subtle aspect that is without truth.
In the teaching on matured butter (*ghṛta*), there are two coarse aspects that are without truth and one subtle aspect that is without truth.
This sutra speaks only of the single, wondrous, and subtle truth of non-arising (*anutpāda-satya*).
It opens up the coarse [truth] as previously described, and so forth.
Question: For what reason do both the Mahayana and Hinayana treatises discuss the truth of non-arising?
Answer: The *Śāstra* states:

"One does not refute the nirvāṇa attained within the minds of the sages; rather, one refutes it because those who have not yet attained it cling to nirvāṇa and give rise to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), like being driven by the impulse of non-arising. Therefore, it is refuted.
This means that there is no truth [in such claims].
Question:
If that is so, then both the attainment and non-attainment of the Hīnayāna are equally refuted; likewise, both the attainment and non-attainment of the Mahāyāna should also be refuted.
Answer:
This is not analogous.
In the Hīnayāna, there still exist distinct afflictions to be eliminated and a distinct principle to be revealed; therefore, although [the path] has been attained, it must still be broken through.
The Middle Way is not like this; how could it be said to be subverted?
Question:
If that is so, the Middle Way should consist of only one true reality (satya), and one should not say that there is no truth.

For those who have not yet attained [realization], delusions arise from grasping at the "middle"; therefore, there must be no truths.
For those who have truly attained, they exist; for those who engage in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), they do not, and so forth.
The Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra, Fascicle Two, Part Two (Miaofa Lianhua Jing Xuan Yi Juan Di Er Xia)
